stem: Why is it recommended to check the mucous membranes and conjunctiva rather than just skin complexion when assessing a child for anemia?

options.text: Skin complexion can be misleading due to natural paleness or general illness
Jaundice is only visible in the mucous membranes
Skin color only changes in acute blood loss
Red blood cells do not circulate near the skin surface in children

explanation: Children may appear pale because they are unwell or have a naturally fair complexion, even if their hemoglobin levels are normal.
rationale: Consider factors like ethnicity, natural coloring, and how the body reacts to general illness beyond blood count.

optionExplanations.A: Children may appear pale because they are unwell or have a naturally fair complexion, even if their hemoglobin levels are normal.
optionExplanations.B: While jaundice is seen in the eyes (scleral icterus), anemia assessment specifically focuses on the vascularity of the membranes to gauge hemoglobin.
optionExplanations.C: Skin color can change in both chronic and acute anemia, but it remains a less reliable indicator than the color of the lips and nail beds.
optionExplanations.D: Red blood cells do circulate in the skin, but peripheral vasoconstriction during illness can make a child look pale regardless of their blood count.
